blocks.h2: Signs Your Arlington Heights Sewer Line Needs Repair
blocks.intro: A clog clears and stays clear. A damaged line keeps telling you something's wrong:

tiles.h3: The Floor Drain Backs Up More Than Once
tiles.body: If the main line has been cleared and the basement floor drain backs up again within a few months, the pipe itself is catching debris.
Air pushing back through the toilet or tub when other fixtures drain means the line isn't moving water freely.

tiles.h3: A Lush Strip in the Lawn
tiles.body: A greener or softer stretch of grass over the sewer path can mean the line is leaking into the soil.
A cracked cast iron drain under the slab or a broken joint outside can let sewer gas into the house.

blocks.h2: Why Sewer Lines Fail in Arlington Heights
blocks.intro: The median home in Arlington Heights was built in 1974, and more than a third went up between 1940 and 1969. Those decades used materials that are now at the end of their life.

items.body: Most homes from the 1940s through the 1960s drain to the street through vitrified clay pipe laid in short sections. Every joint is a place for roots to get in, and parkway trees planted when those blocks were new are now full grown.

items.h3: Cast Iron Under the Basement Floor
items.body: Inside the house, drains from the same era are usually cast iron. After 60 years it rusts from the inside, scales up and can crack along the bottom of the pipe where you can't see it.

items.h3: Combined Sewers in the Older Part of Town
items.body: Parts of older Arlington Heights, mainly near the center of town, have combined sewers that carry both stormwater and wastewater. In a hard rain they fill fast, and a damaged private line gives that water an easy way back into your basement.
Homes from the 1970s and 1980s often have newer pipe materials, but long runs can sag where the soil settled. A sag holds water and paper and turns into a repeat clog.

blocks.h2: How We Handle Sewer Repair in Arlington Heights
blocks.intro: Every sewer repair quote from our Central Road office starts with proof.

steps.body: We run a camera through the line, record it and mark the distance to every crack, root mass or sag. You watch it with us.
One bad joint gets a spot repair. A line that's failing end to end gets lining or replacement, and we show you the footage that supports it.
You get a flat-rate price before any work starts. No add-ons when the job is done.

blocks.h2: How We Repair a Sewer Line
blocks.intro: Once we know what's wrong, there's usually more than one way to fix it. Which method makes sense depends on the pipe's condition, location, and how it failed.
head: Method
What It Involves
Typical Disruption
rows: A resin-coated liner is pulled through the existing pipe and cured in place, creating a new pipe inside the old one.
Minimal digging, usually just small access points
A new pipe is pulled through the old one while a bursting head fractures the old pipe outward to make room.
Minimal digging, works even when the old pipe is badly damaged
The damaged section is dug up and replaced directly.
More digging, but sometimes the only option depending on damage location and access
blocks.note: Many Arlington Heights lines run under a mature parkway tree, a driveway or a detached garage. The camera footage tells us which method fits before anyone talks about digging.

blocks.h2: Sewer Repair Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: My home was built in the 1950s. Is my sewer line clay?
items.preview: Very likely. Clay was standard then. A camera shows what condition it's in.
items.answer: Very likely. Clay pipe was the standard for homes built in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Plenty of clay lines still work, but the joints are where roots and leaks start. A [camera inspection](/arlington-heights/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows exactly where yours stands.

items.q: Can you replace the cast iron drain under my basement floor?
items.preview: Yes. We can line it or replace the damaged section.
items.answer: Yes. Depending on the damage, we can line the old cast iron from the inside or open the floor and replace the bad section. We'll show you the camera footage and explain both options before you decide.

items.q: Can my sewer line be repaired without digging up the yard?
items.preview: Often, yes. Lining and pipe bursting need only small access points.
items.answer: Often, yes. [Trenchless sewer repair](/arlington-heights/trenchless-sewer-repair) relines or replaces the pipe through one or two small openings. A fully collapsed section or a deep sag may still need a spot dig. The camera tells us which applies.

items.q: Who is responsible for the sewer line in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: The homeowner, from the house out to the connection at the main.
items.answer: In Arlington Heights, the village says homeowners maintain their entire sanitary service line, including the connection to the village main. That includes the part under the parkway. If you're not sure where yours connects, the camera locator will show us.

items.q: How much does sewer line repair cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on the damage, the depth and the method. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on what the camera finds: the type of damage, how long and how deep the bad section is, the repair method and what sits on top of the line. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
